\section[quaesō]{quaesō — please (I ask)}

\label{lesson:LA-C03-quaeso}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Latin has no word that simply means \textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{} Instead you say what you're actually doing: \textbf{asking.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{quaesō} — said \emph{KWAI-so} (qu = \textbf{kw}, ae = \textbf{eye}) — literally means \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I ask\textquotedblright{}} or \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I beg.\textquotedblright{}} Romans dropped it into a sentence exactly where English drops \emph{please}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Dā mihi aquam, \textbf{quaesō}} — \textquotedblleft{}Give me water, \textbf{please}\textquotedblright{} (lit. \textquotedblleft{}…I ask\textquotedblright{}).
\end{quote}

It's a worn-down cousin of the verb \textbf{quaerere}, \textquotedblleft{}to seek, to ask\textquotedblright{} — the same root English took for \textbf{query}, \textbf{quest}, \textbf{question}, \textbf{require} and \textbf{inquire}. So \emph{quaesō} is, at heart, \textquotedblleft{}I'm seeking {[}this{]} of you.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Because there's no single word, Latin had a small kit of polite moves — worth meeting so the absence doesn't feel like a gap:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{sīs} — a squeezed \textbf{sī vīs}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{if you wish}\textquotedblright{} (to one person); plural \textbf{sultis} (\emph{sī vultis}). This is the \emph{same} \textquotedblleft{}if you wish\textquotedblright{} strategy French will use in \emph{s'il te plaît}.
  \item \textbf{amābō tē} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I will love you}\textquotedblright{} — a warm, coaxing \textquotedblleft{}please,\textquotedblright{} the way English might say \textquotedblleft{}be a dear.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: \textquotedblleft{}quaesō\textquotedblright{} — \emph{KWAI-so}, \textquotedblleft{}I ask\textquotedblright{}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: in place — \textquotedblleft{}Dā mihi aquam, quaesō\textquotedblright{}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the \textquotedblleft{}if you wish\textquotedblright{} version — \textquotedblleft{}sīs\textquotedblright{} (from \emph{sī vīs}){]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What did Romans literally say instead of \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{quaesō} — \textquotedblleft{}I ask/beg.\textquotedblright{}) What verb is it from, and which English words share that root? (\textbf{quaerere} \textquotedblleft{}to seek\textquotedblright{} — \emph{query, quest, require}.) What does \textbf{sīs} stand for? (\emph{\textbf{sī vīs}}, \textquotedblleft{}if you wish\textquotedblright{} — the same idea French uses in \emph{s'il te plaît}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
